title: The one who spreads and gathers
hookLine: the Creator spreads creation out and draws it back into Himself (Chaupai)

lines: OUT, IN. LUNGS, TIDES, A HEART.
THE RHYTHM AT THE BIGGEST SCALE.
cards: A jellyfish opens, wide and slow, like an umbrella, then closes, pulling itself in, and in that closing it moves forward. Open, close. Spread out, gather in.
Your own chest is doing the same thing right now. Out, in. Lungs, tides, seasons, a beating heart: so much of the living world runs on that one rhythm.
Chaupai takes it and applies it to the biggest thing there is.

teach.h: THE PRAYER STOPS ASKING AND LOOKS.
teach.b: In the middle of Chaupai, the prayer stops asking and simply looks at God. In paraphrase: when the Creator spreads creation out, beings take bodies beyond number.
And when, at any time, you draw it back in, all bodies merge back into you.
The two old words are udkarakh, spreading out, and aakarakh, drawing in. In this picture, the universe is the Creator's long breath. Breathe out, and there are galaxies, rivers, people, ants.

Breathe in, and everything returns to the One it came from. It echoes the Japji, where Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that with a single word the Creator made the vast expanse, and from it a million rivers flowed.
Creation in Sikh thought isn't a machine built once and left to run. It flows out of the One, and it's held in the One the whole time. Why is this in a prayer for protection?
Because it changes what being kept means. If everything came out of the One and returns to the One, nothing that happens to you happens outside God.
Even the drawing in, the ending of things, which frightens us most, is described as merging, not vanishing.
That doesn't make loss painless; Sikhs grieve like everyone else. But it puts loss inside something larger and kinder.
The hand that spread you out is the hand that gathers you in, and your own breath is a small copy of that.

how: Many Sikhs recite these verses of Chaupai Sahib daily, and Sikh teaching describes creation as flowing out from the One and merging back into the One.

o: the breath that keeps a body alive
a teacher who guides the soul home
the Creator, who spreads and gathers all

games.q: spread and gathered — tap the pairs.

s: in Chaupai, the drawing in of creation means everything simply vanishes
the verse says all bodies merge back into the One.
the Japji also pictures creation flowing from the Creator's single word
Guru Nanak says one word made the vast expanse, and rivers flowed from it.
Sikh thought pictures creation as a machine built once and left alone
it flows out of the One and stays held in the One the whole time.

games.q: Chaupai says the Creator spreads creation out into bodies beyond number. what does it say happens when the Creator draws it back in?
o: all bodies merge back into the One.
games.why: jab aakarakh karat ho kabahoon, tum mai milat deh dhar sabhahoon: when you draw it in, all who took bodies merge into you.

practice: Start with the out-breath, long and slow, as if spreading something into the room; pause; then let the in-breath come by itself, gathering back. Don't force it: let it be the rhythm your body already knows.
If you pray, let Waheguru ride on the breath, wahe on the way out, guru on the way in; if not, just watch the two halves of each breath.

wordCard.voice: Kartaar, the Creator. Udkarakh and aakarakh: spreading creation out into countless bodies, and drawing it all back to merge in the One.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kartaar, the Creator, the one Chaupai pictures spreading creation out and gathering it in.

carryVoice: Your line: spread and gathered. The same hand does both, out and in. Until tomorrow.
